passage: The ball rolled under the bench in the school yard in Lyon, and Selin grabbed it before Nour could. "Mine first!" Selin sang, the same way she had sung it all week. Nour shoved her shoulder, hard. Selin sat down on the gravel and her knee went red. When Madame Aubert hurried over, Nour's arms were folded tight. "She was being annoying. She always takes the ball and sings that silly song. She made me do it." Madame Aubert crouched beside Selin first and checked the knee, then looked up at Nour. "Singing is one thing. Pushing is another. Whose hands pushed?" Nour stared at the gravel and kicked a small stone. "Mine," she said at last, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Nour do when Selin grabbed the ball first?
qa.a: Nour shoved her shoulder, hard, and Selin sat down on the gravel with a red knee.

qa.q: Why did it feel fair to Nour to say Selin made her do it?
qa.a: After a whole week of the song, Nour was cross, so calling Selin annoying made the push feel like Selin's fault rather than Nour's own choice.

qa.q: At what moment could Nour have made a different choice, and what could it have been?
qa.a: Right when Selin sang "Mine first!", Nour could have walked away or told Madame Aubert about the ball-grabbing instead of using her hands.

qa.q: How might Selin feel hearing Nour say she made her do it?
qa.a: Sitting there with a sore knee, Selin may feel hurt twice: once by the push and again by being blamed for it 😢.

grounding: Shows a child turning the classmate she pushed into the cause of the push, so her own action feels justified.

passage: At the swimming club, the queue for the diving board was long. Ishita kept splashing water at the boys waiting behind her and laughing. When her turn came, Naveen gave her a push from behind, and she slapped into the water sideways, coughing. The coach blew the whistle and sent Naveen to the bench. Suraj sat down next to him, dripping. "Why'd you do that?" "She was being so irritating, yaar. Splash, splash, splash. She had it coming." Naveen kept his eyes on the pool. "If she'd just stood quietly, nothing would have happened." Suraj watched Ishita climb out, rubbing her ear. "She splashed. You pushed," he said. Naveen didn't answer, but he stopped swinging his legs.

qa.q: Where did Naveen push Ishita?
qa.a: At the swimming club, from behind in the diving-board queue, so she slapped into the water sideways, coughing.

qa.q: What does Naveen's line "If she'd just stood quietly" suggest about how he sees the push?
qa.a: It suggests Naveen feels defensive, blaming Ishita's splashing so he can believe he only reacted and did nothing really wrong.

qa.q: What choice could Naveen have made when the splashing started?
qa.a: He could have told Ishita to stop, moved further back in the queue, or called the coach instead of pushing.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the push differently from Naveen?
qa.a: Suraj separates the two acts: Ishita splashed, but Naveen chose to push, so the push is Naveen's to own.

grounding: Shows a boy justifying a push by insisting the irritating girl brought it on herself.

passage: I'm Sunaina, and I sit two benches behind Vikas in Class 5. On Tuesday, Pallavi kept tapping her ruler on his desk all through drawing period, tap, tap, tap. At break, near the water cooler, Vikas pushed her and she dropped her steel bottle. It rolled all the way to the stairs. Later Vikas told our group, "She was irritating me the whole period. She deserved it." Some boys nodded. I don't know what was really going on inside him. He sounded sure, but he kept looking over at Pallavi, who was sitting alone on the steps. After lunch I saw him pick up her bottle from the stairs and leave it on her desk without saying a word.

qa.q: What happened to Pallavi's steel bottle when Vikas pushed her?
qa.a: She dropped her steel bottle and it rolled all the way to the stairs.

qa.q: Why might Vikas believe Pallavi deserved the push?
qa.a: Her ruler tapping had irritated him the whole period, so he tells himself she started it, which makes the push feel like fair payback.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say when some boys nodded along with Vikas?
qa.a: Sunaina could calmly say the tapping was annoying but the push was Vikas's choice, and suggest he talk to Pallavi or the teacher.

qa.q: What is break time like for Pallavi after the push?
qa.a: Pallavi sits alone on the steps, probably hurt and embarrassed, while the group hears a story that makes her the one to blame 😔.

grounding: A classmate observes a boy claiming the girl he pushed deserved it because she irritated him.

passage:
Monday: In the bus queue, Thomas kept humming the same song and poking Nilofer's water bottle. She shoved him hard. He fell and scraped his knee on the gravel. 'He was being so annoying,' Nilofer told everyone. 'He asked for it.'
Wednesday: Miss Dsouza asked Nilofer to draw what had happened. Nilofer drew Thomas humming, with lots of music notes around his head. 'And where are your hands in the picture?' Miss Dsouza asked. Nilofer drew them small, right at the edge.
Friday: Thomas was still limping a little at PT. Nilofer walked over, cheeks hot. 'Your humming bugged me,' she said. 'But I'm the one who pushed. Sorry.' Thomas shrugged, then offered her half his orange.

qa.q: Where did Thomas scrape his knee?
qa.a: On the gravel in the bus queue.

qa.q: Why did pushing Thomas feel fair to Nilofer on Monday?
qa.a: Nilofer was angry about the humming and poking, so she saw Thomas as the cause; saying 'he asked for it' made the push feel like his fault, not hers.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Nilofer, and why did it work?
qa.a: Miss Dsouza's question about where Nilofer's hands were in the drawing; it did not lecture, it simply made her notice she had left her own action out.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel when Nilofer apologised on Friday?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and a bit surprised that she owned the push instead of blaming his humming; offering half his orange suggests he was ready to make up. 🙂

grounding: A child who pushed an annoying classmate says he asked for it, turning the victim into the cause, before owning the push.

passage:
Ankita, you say Riddhi deserved that push because she kept copying your drawings. Sit here.
When I was nine, in our mohalla in Kanpur, a girl called Kamla always sang loudly on the swing and never gave anyone a turn. One day I tugged the rope, and she fell into the dust. My knees were shaking, but I told my Bauji, 'She asked for it. She's so irritating.'
Bauji didn't shout. He only asked, 'Did her singing push her off the swing, Jyoti?'
I had no answer. Kamla had a torn frock and a cut chin, and all I had was my irritation.
Next morning I took her my red ribbon. Annoying people still don't make our hands move, beta.

qa.q: What happened to Kamla when young Jyoti tugged the rope?
qa.a: She fell into the dust and ended up with a torn frock and a cut chin.

qa.q: Why did young Jyoti say 'She asked for it' even with shaking knees?
qa.a: Jyoti was irritated with Kamla for hogging the swing and wanted the fall to be Kamla's fault; blaming the singing made the tug feel justified, though the shaking knees hint at guilt.

qa.q: Which question changed young Jyoti's thinking, and why?
qa.a: Bauji's 'Did her singing push her off the swing?'; it put the action back on the person who tugged the rope.

qa.q: How might Riddhi see Ankita's reason for the push?
qa.a: Riddhi may feel that copying drawings was a small thing and the push a much bigger one; being blamed for being pushed would likely feel unfair and hurtful.

grounding: An elder recalls pulling a girl off a swing and saying she asked for it, showing how the victim is made the cause.

passage: At the village school in Kodagu, the mud by the handpump was ankle-deep after the rain. Jatin had been humming the same film song all morning, right behind Aadhya in the water line. 'Stop it,' she said. He hummed louder. So she shoved him, hard, and he sat down in the mud, his uniform brown to the waist. Some children laughed. Jatin didn't. He got up with his lip shaking. When Teacher came running, Aadhya folded her arms. 'He was annoying me all morning. He asked for it.' Teacher knelt to check Jatin's hands, then looked at her. 'He was humming. You pushed. Which of those was a choice about someone else's body?' Aadhya kicked at the mud. Teacher sent Jatin for dry clothes, kept Aadhya back to talk, and that evening told Aadhya's mother at the gate.

qa.q: Where was the mud ankle-deep?
qa.a: The mud was ankle-deep by the handpump.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya say Jatin 'asked for it'?
qa.a: She was angry at his humming, and making Jatin the cause let her feel justified instead of guilty about pushing him.

qa.q: What should Aadhya do next time someone annoys her?
qa.a: She could tell him clearly to stop, move away, or ask a teacher, rather than using her hands, and she should apologise to Jatin.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel sitting in the mud?
qa.a: He felt hurt and humiliated, his lip shaking while some children laughed and his uniform was soaked.

grounding: A child who pushed a classmate into the mud insists he was annoying and asked for it, turning the victim into the cause.

passage: At the Saturday football club in Madrid, Pablo wouldn't stop talking about his new boots. 'Real leather. Faster than yours,' he told Chidi for the fifth time on the bench. Chidi's ears went hot. When Pablo leaned over to tap Chidi's old boots, Chidi shoved him off the bench, and Pablo landed on the gravel and scraped his elbow. Coach Marta was there in seconds. 'He was being so annoying,' Chidi said before she could ask. 'Showing off all morning. He deserved it.' Coach Marta cleaned Pablo's elbow first, then sat beside Chidi. 'Pablo was annoying you. That's true. Then you pushed him. Whose choice was the push?' Chidi looked at the gravel. 'Mine,' he muttered. 'But he started it.' 'He started talking. You started pushing.' She told both boys' parents at pickup.

qa.q: What did Pablo keep talking about?
qa.a: Pablo kept talking about his new boots.

qa.q: Why did Chidi say Pablo deserved it?
qa.a: Chidi was angry and embarrassed about his old boots, and blaming Pablo's bragging let him feel justified rather than guilty about the push.

qa.q: What did Coach Marta do well?
qa.a: She cared for Pablo first, agreed the bragging was annoying, made clear that pushing was Chidi's choice, and told both families at pickup.

qa.q: How might Pablo feel after landing on the gravel?
qa.a: Pablo would likely feel hurt and shocked, and perhaps a little embarrassed about bragging, though he didn't deserve to be pushed.

grounding: A child who pushed a bragging teammate off a bench says he deserved it, making the victim the cause of his own act.

passage: In the hostel dining hall, the dinner queue was long, and Sabina slid in two places ahead of Pallavi to stand with her friend. 'Oi, back of the line,' Pallavi said. Sabina ignored her. Pallavi pushed her in the back, hard, and Sabina stumbled into the steel counter and dropped her plate with a clang. The whole hall went quiet. Sabina held her wrist, eyes wet. When the warden, Mrs Thomas, came over, Pallavi said quickly, 'She cut the line. She always does. She asked for it.' Mrs Thomas checked Sabina's wrist and sent her with a senior to the sick room. Then she turned to Pallavi. 'Cutting the line is wrong. Pushing someone into a counter is also wrong. Only one of them could break a wrist.' Pallavi's face went red. 'My office after dinner,' Mrs Thomas said. 'And I'm calling your mother tonight.'

qa.q: What did Sabina drop?
qa.a: Sabina dropped her plate with a clang.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi say Sabina 'asked for it'?
qa.a: Pallavi was angry about the line-cutting, and blaming Sabina made the push feel justified instead of shameful.

qa.q: What could Pallavi have done when Sabina cut the line?
qa.a: Pallavi could have told the warden or a senior instead of pushing.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after stumbling into the counter?
qa.a: Sabina was hurt and shaken, holding her wrist with wet eyes in front of the silent hall.

grounding: A child who pushed a classmate into a counter says she cut the line and asked for it, turning the victim into the cause.

passage:
Monday: In the lunch line, Chetan kept humming the same cartoon song right behind Mehak. She told him to stop twice. The third time, she shoved him and he fell against the water cooler, scraping his elbow.
Tuesday: Mrs Iyer asked her to explain. Mehak folded her arms. “He was being so annoying. He asked for it. If he'd stopped humming, nothing would have happened.” It sounded completely fair to her.
Friday: Before the maths test, Mehak caught herself tapping her pencil over and over. Her bench partner sighed loudly. Mehak stopped, cheeks warm. Annoying, she thought. But nobody pushed me.
At break she found Chetan, looked at his plaster and said, “Sorry about your elbow.”

qa.q: What happened to Chetan's elbow on Monday?
qa.a: He fell against the water cooler and scraped his elbow when Mehak shoved him.

qa.q: Why did Mehak's explanation on Tuesday feel fair to her?
qa.a: She was still angry, and making Chetan's humming the cause let her feel justified instead of guilty about the push.

qa.q: What could Mehak try the next time someone annoys her?
qa.a: She could walk away or tell a teacher, because being annoyed is real but it doesn't make pushing okay.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel hearing that he “asked for it”?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and blamed twice, once by the push and again by being told it was his own fault.

grounding: The passage shows a child who pushed a classmate calling him annoying so the push seems deserved.

passage:
Varun, you say Ishan “deserved” that push because he kept boasting. Let me, your Nazia Nani, tell you something I did.
When I was eleven in Lucknow, a girl called Rehana sat next to me. She always corrected my spellings, loudly, in front of the class. One day, in the courtyard, I pushed her into the puddle by the hand-pump. Her uniform was soaked.
When the headmistress called me, I said, “She's such a know-all. She was asking for it.” I truly believed it. Rehana was the problem, not my hands.
Then my own Abba said, very quietly, “Did Rehana push you, Nazia?” I had no answer.
I went to her house that evening with my own dry dupatta to lend her. She took it. We stayed friends for sixty years.

qa.q: Where did young Nazia push Rehana?
qa.a: She pushed her into the puddle by the hand-pump in the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did young Nazia truly believe Rehana was asking for it?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and angry at being corrected in front of the class, so blaming Rehana let her feel her push was justified.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Nazia make the choice that changed things?
qa.a: After her Abba's quiet question, she chose to go to Rehana's house that evening with a dry dupatta to make amends.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt standing in her soaked uniform?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt shocked and embarrassed, and hurt that Nazia called it her fault.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a child blaming the classmate she pushed for being annoying, until a question returns the responsibility.

passage:
The school bus was stuck in rain traffic near the flyover, windows fogged, forty children packed in and the conductor shouting over the thunder.
Tenzin, behind Kamal, kept kicking the back of his seat. Tap, tap, tap. Kamal turned twice. “Stop it.”
The third time, Kamal stood and shoved Tenzin hard. Tenzin's head bumped the window frame and his eyes filled.
The conductor pulled them apart. “Why?”
“He was so annoying! He kept kicking. He deserved it,” Kamal said, breathing fast. Everyone was hot and sticky and cross; it felt obvious to him.
The conductor held Tenzin's head gently, checking the bump. “Kicking a seat is wrong,” the conductor said. “Pushing a head into glass is a different kind of wrong. That one's yours.”
Kamal sat down, still angry, but his hands were trembling now.

qa.q: What did Tenzin keep doing on the bus?
qa.a: Tenzin kept kicking the back of Kamal's seat, tap, tap, tap.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel sure Tenzin deserved the push?
qa.a: Kamal was hot, cross and angry, so Tenzin's kicking felt like the whole cause, making his own push feel justified.

qa.q: What could Kamal do differently on a crowded, rainy ride next time?
qa.a: He could ask the conductor to move him or deal with the kicking, instead of pushing.

qa.q: How did the conductor see the push differently from Kamal?
qa.a: The conductor saw two separate wrongs and held Kamal responsible for the push, not Tenzin.

grounding: The passage shows a child on a cramped rainy bus justifying a push by saying the annoying classmate deserved it.

passage: In the rainy week before Raksha Bandhan, Class 4 was stuck indoors at break. Sudha kept singing the same song, loudly, near Devika's desk. Devika told her to stop twice. The third time, Devika pushed her. Sudha fell against a bench and hurt her elbow. Mrs Nair, the class teacher, checked the elbow and sent Sudha to the nurse with a friend. Then she sat with Devika. "She was so annoying, ma'am. She asked for it." "Did Sudha ask you to push her?" "No. But she made me." "She was annoying. But who decided to push?" Devika's lip trembled. "Me." "Annoying is a reason to walk away or call me. Never to push." Before home time, Devika went to the nurse's room and said sorry.

qa.q: What did Sudha hurt when she fell?
qa.a: She hurt her elbow.

qa.q: Why did Devika say Sudha "asked for it"?
qa.a: Devika was angry and felt justified, and blaming Sudha's singing made the push feel like Sudha's fault instead of her own choice.

qa.q: What did Mrs Nair do that helped Devika take responsibility?
qa.a: She first cared for Sudha, then agreed Sudha was annoying but asked who decided to push, and gave Devika better choices for next time.

qa.q: What was the afternoon like for Sudha?
qa.a: Sudha was hurt and probably upset, needing the nurse after being pushed for singing.

grounding: During a rainy festival week a girl pushes an annoying classmate and says she asked for it, turning the victim into the cause.

passage:
"Trisha, why is Jomon's knee bleeding?"
"He fell, Mamma."
"He fell, or you pushed him?"
"...I pushed him. But he deserved it."
"Why?"
"At Christmas carol practice he kept singing louder than everyone and showing off. He was being so annoying. He asked for it."
"Did he ask you to push him?"
"No. But he was annoying."
"Lots of people are annoying. Is everyone who is annoying supposed to be pushed?"
"No."
"So who chose to push?"
Trisha twisted the edge of her sweater. "Me."
"How do you think Jomon felt?"
"Bad. He cried in front of everyone."
"What can you do now?"
"Say sorry. And give him a plaster."
"Let's do it now, before dinner."
They walked across to Jomon's flat with the first-aid box.

qa.q: Where was Jomon showing off?
qa.a: At Christmas carol practice, singing louder than everyone.

qa.q: Why did Trisha think Jomon deserved to be pushed?
qa.a: Trisha felt annoyed and angry, and saying he asked for it made the push feel fair and not her fault.

qa.q: How did Mamma help Trisha see her choice?
qa.a: Mamma asked whether annoying people should all be pushed and who chose to push, so Trisha named her own part and went to apologise that evening.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after being pushed?
qa.a: Jomon felt hurt and embarrassed, crying in front of everyone.

grounding: A girl who pushed a showing-off classmate at carol practice says he deserved it, turning the victim into the cause, until her mother asks who chose.

passage:
The Holi I was eleven, Simran twice pushed ahead of me in the colour-stall queue. The second time I shoved her so hard she fell in the wet colour and scraped her hand. Her mother came running. And I heard myself say, "She asked for it. She kept cutting the line."
I believed it. In my head she had made me do it.
My father didn't shout. He just said, "Nilesh, she cut the line. What did you do?" I said, "I pushed her." "And who is responsible for the push?" I didn't want to answer.
It took me years to see what I'd done. I had turned Simran into the cause so I didn't have to feel bad. The line-cutting was hers. The push was mine.
— Nilesh

qa.q: What happened to Simran's hand when she fell?
qa.a: She scraped her hand.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh believe Simran was the reason for the push?
qa.a: Nilesh felt angry and wanted to feel justified, so making Simran the cause protected Nilesh from feeling guilty.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's father ask that helped separate the two acts?
qa.a: He asked what Nilesh did and who was responsible for the push, pulling apart Simran's line-cutting from Nilesh's own choice.

qa.q: What might Simran's mother have felt running over?
qa.a: She probably felt alarmed and upset seeing her daughter pushed into the wet colour.

grounding: An adult recalls pushing a girl who cut the Holi queue and saying she asked for it, turning the victim into the cause.

passage:
Playground duty, week before Diwali: note for the Class 5 file.
During the rangoli break, Tanvir pushed Bidisha off the bench and she scraped her elbow on the stones. I took her to the first-aid room myself; it was a small scrape, but she was shaking.
When I sat down with Tanvir, he folded his arms. "She was annoying. She kept saying our rangoli was crooked. She asked for it."
I asked, "What did Bidisha do with her hands?"
"Nothing. She just talked."
"And what did you do with yours?"
He was quiet, then said, "Pushed."
Next steps: Tanvir will apologise tomorrow and help redraw the rangoli with Bidisha's team, and I phoned both families this evening.

qa.q: What happened to Bidisha's elbow?
qa.a: She scraped it on the stones when Tanvir pushed her off the bench.

qa.q: Why does "She asked for it" feel true to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir felt angry and irritated about the crooked-rangoli comments, and blaming Bidisha lets him feel justified instead of guilty about the push.

qa.q: How did the adult's questions help Tanvir?
qa.a: Asking what each child did with their hands separated talking from pushing, so Tanvir named his own action; an apology, a repair job and calls home followed.

qa.q: What was the break like for Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha was pushed, scraped her elbow and was shaking, so it was frightening and painful for her, whatever she had said about the rangoli.

grounding: A child says the classmate he pushed was annoying and deserved it, turning the victim into the cause.
